3.1.l: Pediatric Hip — Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip: Treatment by Age
3.1.b:
Treatment of developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) rests on one aim, so the aim comes first.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is the aim of treating DDH?"
- "A **concentric reduction**, gained as early as possible and then kept."
- "A concentric head is the strongest stimulus for acetabular growth."
- "The method depends on the **age** at diagnosis."

### Natural History of the Unstable Hip
The neonatal unstable hip usually settles, but not always.
- Of Barlow-positive newborns, **60%** stabilise in the first week
[[FIG: Fig 3.1 · 3.1
- By 2 months, **88%** have stabilised
- About **12%** persist as a dislocation (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- So every unstable newborn hip is treated: 100% treated for the 12%

#### Which Course Is Worst
- A reduced but dysplastic hip is a small problem
- A high, fully dislocated hip may stay painless for years
- **Subluxation** is the worst course and predicts arthritis
[[FIG: Fig 3.2 · 3.1
- Labral shear arrests acetabular growth instead of stimulating it

### Aims of Treatment
Reduction changes no anatomy by itself; growth does the remodelling.
- Aim: **concentric reduction**, never partial or "nearly there"
- No concentric reduction → the hip will not develop normally
- Head and acetabulum then stimulate each other as the child grows
- Remodelling is fastest in the **first 3 years** of life

#### Two Growth Spurts
- First 3 years: reduction drives acetabular development
- Second spurt at maturity: a good hip may show **late dysplasia**
- So every treated hip is followed to skeletal maturity

MEMORY HOOK — the shy socket
- The acetabulum is a shy socket: it only grows when the head sits right in the middle of it.

3.2.l: Pediatric Hip — Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip: Treatment by Age
3.2.b:
Age at diagnosis picks the tool; the aim never changes.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you treat DDH by age?"
- "Under **6 months**: Pavlik harness."
- "**6–18 months**: closed reduction, or open reduction if it fails."
- "Over **18 months**: open reduction, usually with osteotomy."

### Age Groups
Campbell uses five groups; the Handbook and Miller follow them closely
[[FIG: Fig 3.3 · 3.2

| Age | First choice | If it fails |
|---|---|---|
| **0–6 months** | Pavlik harness | closed reduction, or a rigid abduction brace |
| **6–18 months** | EUA, arthrogram, closed reduction, spica | open reduction |
| **18 months–3 years** | open reduction ± pelvic osteotomy | — |
| **3–8 years** | open reduction + femoral shortening + pelvic osteotomy | — |
| **>8 years** | salvage, or leave unreduced (bilateral) | THA in adulthood |

- EUA = examination under anaesthesia; THA = total hip arthroplasty
- Pathology, not age alone, decides between closed and open

#### The Lecturer's Preference at 6–18 Months
- The Handbook makes closed reduction first-line at 6–18 months (Handbook)
- Prof Abdel-Ghani prefers to wait to about 1 year
- Then: one operation of open reduction, capsulorrhaphy and Dega osteotomy
- Pelvic osteotomies in detail → 04 Pelvic Osteotomies

PITFALL — closed or open at 6–18 months?
- Textbooks start with closed reduction; Prof Abdel-Ghani prefers open reduction plus osteotomy at about 1 year.
- Say → "Closed reduction first, done correctly; open reduction if it fails."

3.3.l: Pediatric Hip — Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip: Treatment by Age
3.3.b:
The harness is a dynamic flexion–abduction orthosis; it works only while the hip is young and supple.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how does the Pavlik harness work?"
- "Hip **flexion** relaxes the hamstrings; gentle **abduction** lets the head dock."
- "It blocks extension and adduction, but allows movement."
- "No reduction in **3 weeks** → stop it."

### Indications
Treat the unstable or dislocated hip, and the dysplasia that has not settled.
- **Ortolani-positive** hip (dislocated, reducible): treat at once
- **Barlow-positive** hip (reduced, dislocatable): treat at once
- Dysplasia on ultrasound still present at 6 weeks: treat
- Ortolani-negative hip: a trial is allowed, with a high failure rate

### Types of Splints
"Pavlik method" means any brace with the same mechanism
[[FIG: Fig 3.4 · 3.3

| Splint | Movement | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Von Rosen splint** | none: fixed like a cast | historic |
| **Tübingen brace** | some | flexion 90–110°, abduction 40–50° |
| **Pavlik harness** | controlled | the classic, still first choice |
| **Triple nappy** | — | abandoned: costly and weak |
[[FIG: Fig 3.5 · 3.3

### Pavlik Harness
A chest strap, two shoulder straps and two stirrups make the whole device
[[FIG: Fig 3.6 · 3.3

#### Application
- Child supine; chest strap at the **nipple line**, three fingers loose
- **Anteromedial strap** sets flexion: **90–100°** (Campbell)
- **Posterolateral strap** loose: it stops adduction past neutral
- It must never force abduction; knees 3–5 cm apart at full adduction
- Tension is set at the **proximal tibia**, not the foot

#### Common Errors
- Chest strap on the abdomen → poor control of the limbs
- Strap clips too far anterior → flexion only, no abduction
[[FIG: Fig 3.7 · 3.3
- Re-attach the anterior strap at the **anterior axillary line**

#### Mechanism of Reduction
- Knee and hip flexion **relax the hamstrings**, which keep the hip out
- Adduction and extension are blocked; the child kicks freely
- Repeated gentle abduction stretches the adductors → the head reduces
- Parents: the baby may wake crying when the hip slips in

### Follow-Up and Weaning
Clinical examination and ultrasound monitor the harness, not routine films
[[FIG: Fig 3.8 · 3.3
- Worn **23–24 h** a day until Barlow and Ortolani are negative
- Review every 1–2 weeks and adjust straps for growth
- Ultrasound after starting, after major adjustment, and when stable
- Then about **6 weeks** more full time (Miller)

#### Stopping the Harness
- Old rule: wean 2–3 h a day, then nights only (Handbook)
- Recent view: stop at once, without weaning (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- Stop when stable, alpha angle ≈**60°**, and over half the head covered
- AP pelvis film at 6 months, when the head ossifies
[[FIG: Fig 3.9 · 3.3

MEMORY HOOK — the three-week rent
- The Pavlik rents the hip for three weeks: no reduction by then, the lease ends.

### Failure of the Pavlik Harness
A harness that does not reduce the hip starts to damage it.

#### When to Stop
- No reduction within **3 weeks** → stop (Miller)
- Campbell allows 3–6 weeks for persistent subluxation
- Next step: closed or open reduction
[[FIG: Fig 3.10 · 3.3
- A rigid abduction brace may still reduce some hips
[[FIG: Fig 3.11 · 3.3

#### Pavlik Harness Disease
- The head pushed on the posterior wall erodes it
- It flattens the head and crushes the labrum
- It erodes the pelvis above the acetabulum (Miller)
- Later closed reduction becomes harder

#### Risk Factors for Failure
| Factor | Source |
|---|---|
| **Ortolani-negative** (irreducible) hip | Campbell, Miller |
| **Bilateral** dislocation | Campbell, Miller |
| Start after **7 weeks** of age | Miller |
| Femoral nerve palsy during treatment | Campbell |
| Acetabular index ≥36° · coverage <20% | Campbell |
| Male sex | Prof Abdel-Ghani |

### Contraindications
A harness needs a supple hip and working muscles.
- **Teratologic** dislocation: Pavlik will fail
- Muscle imbalance: myelomeningocele, paralysis
- Stiff joints: **arthrogryposis**; marked ligamentous laxity
- The crawling child over 6 months: success falls sharply

### Complications
Two complications matter: nerve palsy and avascular necrosis.

#### Femoral Nerve Palsy
- Incidence ≈**2.5%**; most appear in the first week (Badrinath 2021)
- Cause: hyperflexion of the hip
- Sign: no active knee extension against gravity
- Heavier, older infants are at higher risk
- Remove the harness until the quadriceps recovers; reapply without hyperflexion

#### Avascular Necrosis
- Avascular necrosis (AVN) comes from **forced abduction** (Campbell)
- Never abduct beyond the safe zone to gain stability
- Campbell puts palsy and AVN together at <1%

PITFALL — the abduction angle in the harness
- The lecture said abduction over 60°; textbooks warn that forced abduction causes AVN.
- Say → "Flexion 90–100°, abduction gentle and free, never forced; the strap only blocks adduction."

3.4.l: Pediatric Hip — Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip: Treatment by Age
3.4.b:
Closed reduction is a planned operation under anaesthesia, never a quick abduct-and-cast.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you do a closed reduction?"
- "EUA, **arthrogram**, gentle reduction, safe zone, ± adductor tenotomy."
- "Spica in the **human position**; confirm with CT or MRI."
- "Accept only a concentric, stable reduction."

### Steps of Closed Reduction
Each step answers one question: is the head truly in?

#### Examination Under Anaesthesia
- Muscles relaxed: is the head reducible?
- Not reducible → closed reduction is impossible → open reduction

#### Arthrography
- Dye outlines the cartilage head, labrum and acetabulum
[[FIG: Fig 3.12 · 3.4
- A clunk is not proof: the head may ride over a **neolimbus**
[[FIG: Fig 3.13 · 3.4
- Dynamic screening shows dislocation and reduction in turn
[[FIG: Fig 3.14 · 3.4
- Medial dye pool ≤**5 mm** = acceptable reduction (Campbell)
- A wider pool means soft tissue in the way, such as the ligamentum teres
[[FIG: Fig 3.15 · 3.4
- No ossific nucleus on the C-arm → judge by the arthrogram
- **Thorn sign**: a normal labrum, not inverted

#### Ramsey Safe Zone
- The arc between redislocation in adduction and maximum abduction
[[FIG: Fig 3.16 · 3.4
- Subtract 10° from each end; the rest is the safe zone

| Source | Acceptable safe zone |
|---|---|
| Campbell | minimum 20°, preferably 45° |
| Handbook | ≥30° |
| Miller | narrow if <40° → adductor tenotomy |

- Narrow zone → **adductor tenotomy**, then re-test
- Still narrow → open reduction

#### Adductor Tenotomy
- Mild contracture: percutaneous tenotomy
- Severe or long-standing: open tenotomy through a small transverse cut
- Closed reduction plus tenotomy is still a closed reduction

MEMORY HOOK — the clunk liar
- A clunk is a smooth liar: the head can climb the neolimbus and still be out. Trust the dye, not the noise.

### Hip Spica Cast
The cast holds the reduction in the "human position" of Salter
[[FIG: Fig 3.17 · 3.4
- About **95°** flexion and **40–45°** abduction (Campbell)
- Mould over the greater trochanter; leave room for hygiene
- Neutral rotation: turning the feet rotates the knees, not the hip
- 3 months in cast; change under anaesthesia at **6 weeks** (Campbell)
- The Handbook gives 6 weeks only
- Lax at 3 months → a further 3 months

### Imaging After Reduction
A plain film through a cast cannot show a cartilage head.
- **CT** or **MRI** confirms the reduction
[[FIG: Fig 3.18 · 3.4
- MRI shows cartilage and avoids radiation
[[FIG: Fig 3.19 · 3.4
- CT specificity 96%, MRI 100%
- Persistent inverted labrum on MRI usually still does well

### Pre-Reduction Traction
Traction is the most disputed step in this age group
[[FIG: Fig 3.20 · 3.4
- Longitudinal traction alone: success ≈57–58%, almost abandoned
[[FIG: Fig 3.21 · 3.4
- **Overhead** traction with gradual abduction: 74–92% (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
[[FIG: Fig 3.22 · 3.4
- It needs special frames and days in hospital
[[FIG: Fig 3.23 · 3.4
- Campbell: role controversial; skeletal traction is not indicated
- The Handbook calls it abandoned

PITFALL — is traction still used?
- Prof Abdel-Ghani calls guided overhead traction the key to good closed results; Campbell calls it controversial.
- Say → "Traction is controversial; femoral shortening has replaced it in the older child."

### Outcome of Closed Reduction
Success means a concentric hip, not a reduced film.
- Redislocation on post-reduction imaging: **5–15%** (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- Later pelvic osteotomy for residual dysplasia: **66–85%**
- One 31-year series needed extra osteotomy in only 8.5% (Badrinath 2021)
- AVN after closed reduction may reach **25%** (Campbell)
- Earlier reduction gives better remodelling and fewer complications
- Never fix a closed reduction with a **K-wire**: a hip that needs it is not reduced

Open reduction removes the blocks that keep the head out; nothing should be forced.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what blocks reduction in DDH?"
- "Outside: **iliopsoas tendon**, hourglass capsule, adductors."
- "Inside: **ligamentum teres**, pulvinar, transverse acetabular ligament, inverted limbus."
- "Remove them all; the head then reduces without force."

### Indications
Open reduction is chosen by pathology, not only age.
- Failed closed reduction, or an unstable reduction
- Safe zone still narrow after tenotomy
- Obstructive limbus on arthrogram
- First choice from **18 months** on

### Obstacles to Reduction
Know them as two lists: outside and inside the joint
[[FIG: Fig 3.24 · 3.5

| Extra-articular | Intra-articular |
|---|---|
| **Iliopsoas tendon** across the capsule | hypertrophied **ligamentum teres** |
| hourglass **capsular constriction** | fibrofatty **pulvinar** |
| tight adductors | contracted **transverse acetabular ligament** |
| — | inverted, hypertrophied **limbus** |

### Medial (Ludloff) Approach
Quick, bloodless and direct, but it cannot tighten the capsule
[[FIG: Fig 3.25 · 3.5

#### Technique
- **Transverse** incision over adductor longus, in the skin lines
[[FIG: Fig 3.26 · 3.5
- Divide **adductor longus**
[[FIG: Fig 3.27 · 3.5
- Pectineus above, adductor brevis below; protect the anterior obturator nerve
[[FIG: Fig 3.28 · 3.5
- Find the lesser trochanter and divide the **iliopsoas** tendon
[[FIG: Fig 3.29 · 3.5
- Protect the **medial circumflex femoral artery** (MFCA) below the capsule
[[FIG: Fig 3.30 · 3.5
- Open the capsule; divide the transverse acetabular ligament; reduce
[[FIG: Fig 3.31 · 3.5
- Wenger: shorten the ligamentum teres and suture it to the transverse ligament

#### Limitations
- No capsulorrhaphy and no pelvic osteotomy
- AVN **10–20%** in some series (Campbell)
- A high dislocation in a walking child cannot be brought down
- Indication: infants **6–18 months** (Campbell); up to 12 months (Miller)

### Anterior (Smith-Petersen) Approach
The workhorse: it reaches the capsule, allows capsulorrhaphy and a pelvic osteotomy
[[FIG: Fig 3.32 · 3.5

#### Exposure
- First a **percutaneous adductor tenotomy**
[[FIG: Fig 3.33 · 3.5
- The blade cuts adductor longus only
[[FIG: Fig 3.34 · 3.5
- **Bikini incision** along the iliac crest, below the bony ridge
[[FIG: Fig 3.35 · 3.5
- Interval: sartorius medially, **tensor fasciae latae** laterally
[[FIG: Fig 3.36 · 3.5
- Split the iliac apophysis; it leads into the right plane
[[FIG: Fig 3.37 · 3.5
- Periosteal elevator aims medially and inferiorly
[[FIG: Fig 3.38 · 3.5
- A transverse push enters the sacroiliac joint
[[FIG: Fig 3.39 · 3.5
- Packing gives haemostasis and periosteal stripping
[[FIG: Fig 3.40 · 3.5

#### Release
- Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve appears in the interval: protect it
[[FIG: Fig 3.41 · 3.5
- **Iliopsoas** tendon: divide the tendon, keep the muscle
[[FIG: Fig 3.42 · 3.5
- Roll the muscle until the tendon is delivered on an angled clamp
[[FIG: Fig 3.43 · 3.5
- Divide **rectus femoris** at the anterior inferior iliac spine (AIIS)

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "why shorten the femur in DDH?"
- "To reduce the head **without tension**, so less AVN and redislocation."
- "It replaces pre-reduction traction in the older child."
- "Shorten for tension; derotate a little; varus only for true valga."

### Femoral Shortening
The decision is made on the table, when the head will not reduce gently.

#### Values of Femoral Shortening
- Allows reduction without force
- Less pressure on the head → less AVN
- Less stretch on the sciatic and femoral nerves
- Allows a little derotation in the same cut
- The resected bone grafts the pelvic osteotomy

#### Technique
- Subtrochanteric osteotomy through a lateral incision
[[FIG: Fig 3.62 · 3.6
- Fix the plate and two proximal screws first, then cut
- Reduce the head; the fragment overlap = the shortening
[[FIG: Fig 3.63 · 3.6
- Usually **1–3 cm** (Campbell)
[[FIG: Fig 3.64 · 3.6
- Plan it on the film: head top to triradiate cartilage
- Derotation 15–45° may be needed
[[FIG: Fig 3.65 · 3.6

#### Derotation Danger
- Capsulorrhaphy, pelvic osteotomy and derotation all turn the head back
- Together in excess → iatrogenic **posterior dislocation**
[[FIG: Fig 3.66 · 3.6
- A head that is "deep and never comes out" may be out posteriorly
- So test stability after the pelvic osteotomy before derotating

### Toddler 18 Months to 3 Years
Remodelling power falls after 18 months, so reduction alone is no longer enough.
- Open reduction first; no trial of closed reduction (Handbook)
- Add a pelvic osteotomy, or a femoral one where the deformity lies
- After 3 years, both femoral and pelvic osteotomies are usually needed

### Child 3 to 8 Years
Outcomes worsen with each year of delay.
- Open reduction + femoral shortening + pelvic osteotomy: one stage
[[FIG: Fig 3.67 · 3.6
- Traction alone here: AVN 54%, redislocation 31% (Campbell)
- Femoral osteotomy with an untouched pelvis is illogical
[[FIG: Fig 3.68 · 3.6

### Varus Osteotomy in DDH
Apparent coxa valga is usually anteversion seen on an externally rotated film
[[FIG: Fig 3.69 · 3.6
- The lesser trochanter looks prominent; the neck is seen end-on
- An internal-rotation view shows a normal neck–shaft angle
- Needless varus → functional coxa vara, weak abductors, no acetabular growth
[[FIG: Fig 3.70 · 3.6
- Hold the reduction by technique, never by a K-wire

- Prof Abdel-Ghani never adds a varus cut; Campbell and the Handbook use varus derotation for a true increased neck–shaft angle.
- Say → "Shorten for tension, derotate a little; varus only if internal rotation still shows valgus."

MEMORY HOOK — the shy valgus
- DDH valgus is camera-shy: turn the leg in, and the "valga" disappears.

- Closed reduction fails; Pavlik is contraindicated

- One side first; the other side about **2 weeks** later
- Total cast time falls to about 2.5 months
- Simultaneous bilateral osteotomies bleed heavily

AVN is the most serious complication of any DDH treatment, closed or open.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what complications follow reduction?"
- "**AVN**, also called proximal femoral growth disturbance (PFGD)."
- "**Redislocation** and **residual acetabular dysplasia**."
- "Stiffness, fracture, and late dysplasia at adolescence."

### Proximal Femoral Growth Disturbance
Many now prefer "growth disturbance", because true necrosis is rarely proven.
- Incidence <5% to almost 50% (Campbell)
- Up to 10–35% even after closed reduction
- It appears on treated and even untreated sides
- The ossific nucleus offers little protection; do not delay reduction for it (Campbell)

#### Causes
- Forced reduction under tension
- Extreme abduction: the **frog position** in cast
- Vascular injury: the MFCA in the medial approach
- Pressure and post-operative hyperaemia

### Salter Criteria
Salter's criteria diagnose AVN after reduction (Salter, 1969).
- Failure of the ossific nucleus to appear within 1 year
- Failure of an existing nucleus to grow within 1 year
- **Broadening of the femoral neck** within 1 year
- Increased density, then fragmentation of the head
- Residual deformity after re-ossification: coxa magna, plana, vara, short neck

### Kalamchi–MacEwen Classification
The classification tells which part of the physis is hit
[[FIG: Fig 3.74 · 3.7

| Type | Damage | Result |
|---|---|---|
| **I** | ossific nucleus only | small, mottled nucleus; recovers |
| **II** | **lateral** physis | lateral tether → valgus tilt, coxa valga |
| **III** | **central** physis | short neck, coxa breva |
| **IV** | **whole** head and physis | severe deformity, early closure |
[[FIG: Fig 3.75–3.76 · 3.7

- Type II appears late, near adolescence
[[FIG: Fig 3.77 · 3.7
- The head stays centred for years before the valgus shows
[[FIG: Fig 3.78 · 3.7
- Type III shortens the neck early and deforms the acetabulum
[[FIG: Fig 3.79 · 3.7
- Type IV damages the whole head and physis
[[FIG: Fig 3.80 · 3.7
- Bucholz–Ogden is a similar four-type system
[[FIG: Fig 3.81 · 3.7

PITFALL — Kalamchi type IV
- The lecture called type IV "medial physis, coxa vara"; it is really total head and physeal damage.
- Say → "I nucleus, II lateral physis, III central physis, IV the whole head and physis."

MEMORY HOOK — the lighthouse
- Kalamchi is a lighthouse moving across the physis: I the lamp only, II the lateral shore, III the centre, IV the whole island.

#### Early Look, Late Outcome
- Early appearance does **not** predict the final head
[[FIG: Fig 3.82 · 3.7
- A Perthes-like head after open reduction may remodel to normal
[[FIG: Fig 3.83 · 3.7
- The class may not be clear until 4–6 years of age

#### Sequelae and Treatment
- Head deformity, residual dysplasia, trochanteric overgrowth, limb-length difference
[[FIG: Fig 3.84 · 3.7
- Overgrown trochanter → trochanteric advancement
- Early pelvic osteotomy (1–3 years after insult) gives better heads

### Redislocation
Redislocation is a technical failure until proven otherwise
[[FIG: Fig 3.85 · 3.7
- Least after open reduction + capsulorrhaphy + pelvic osteotomy
- Most after closed reduction
- Early redislocation: no immediate re-operation on a stiff hip
- Re-do open reduction is very hard: AVN up to 50% (Miller)

### Stiffness After the Cast
The hip comes out of the cast stiff in flexion and abduction.
- No physiotherapy: the bone is **osteopenic**
- Forced adduction may cause a subtrochanteric fracture
- The child regains movement alone; unilateral cases recover faster
- Prevent falls; abduction makes the leg look longer for a while

### Inverted Labrum
An inverted labrum is usually iatrogenic, from a forced closed reduction.
- Never excise the labrum; never make many radial cuts
- At most one radial incision, then evert it with a hook

- "Improving acetabular index → observe; plateau → pelvic osteotomy."
- "Late dysplasia can appear at the adolescent growth spurt."

### Residual Acetabular Dysplasia
Most common after closed reduction and after open reduction alone.
- Yearly AP pelvis: is the acetabular index falling?
[[FIG: Fig 3.86 · 3.8
- Improving → observe; most remodelling ends by 5–6 years
- No cut-off: keep following
- Coverage = acetabular roof over the head; congruence = fit of head and socket
- Plateau, or any subluxation → pelvic osteotomy → 04 Pelvic Osteotomies

### Late-Developing Dysplasia
A hip that looked normal at 5 years can fail at 13.
- The second growth spurt may unmask dysplasia
- Never discharge at 5 years; follow to the end of growth
- Late acetabular dysplasia in detail → 04 Pelvic Osteotomies

MEMORY HOOK — the school report
- A treated hip brings a school report every year until it graduates: maturity, not age 5.

[[FIG: Fig 3.86 · 3.8

- Coverage = acetabular roof over the head; congruence = fit of head and socket

3.8.2.l: Pediatric Hip — Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip: Treatment by Age
3.8.2.b:
A hip that looked normal at 5 years can fail at 13.
- The second growth spurt may unmask dysplasia
- Never discharge at 5 years; follow to the end of growth
- Late acetabular dysplasia in detail → 04 Pelvic Osteotomies

MEMORY HOOK — the school report
- A treated hip brings a school report every year until it graduates: maturity, not age 5.
